summary: Defines how the Extensible Provisioning Protocol is used to provision and manage host names stored in a shared registry. It specifies the command syntax and semantics for host objects. It obsoletes an earlier version and is an Internet Standard.

eli5.summary: This is the EPP rulebook chapter about computer names, such as name servers, saying how to add or update them in the registry.

questions: what is an epp host object
what is a subordinate host in epp
can you transfer an epp host object
what does epp result code 1001 mean
subtitle: How a domain registry stores and manages host names, such as name servers, over EPP.

tldr.problem: A shared registry that holds domain names also needs a standard way to store the host names (usually name servers) that domains point to, so registrars can manage them with the same protocol.
tldr.mechanism: The mapping defines a host object with a name, optional IP addresses and status values, and says how the EPP check, info, create, delete and update commands apply to it, all in XML.
tldr.outcome: It is an Internet Standard that obsoletes RFC 4932. Hosts are not renewed or transferred directly; they follow their parent domain.

today: RFC 5732 is an Internet Standard (STD 69) published in August 2009. It obsoletes RFC 4932, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: What a Host Object Is
sections.content:
RFC 5732 describes an Internet host name mapping for version 1.0 of the Extensible Provisioning Protocol (EPP). It is written in XML with XML Schema, and it only makes sense next to the base protocol in RFC 5730, which defines the command and response structures.

A host object is a host name stored in a shared central repository. Its attributes can be viewed and modified by the sponsoring client or by the server.

XML is case sensitive, so the document says its examples MUST be read in the character case shown.
sections.eli5: A host object is one entry in the registry's address book for a computer's name. Only the company in charge of the entry, or the registry itself, can change it.

sections.title: Hosts and Their Parent Domains
sections.content:
The mapping assumes a host name object is subordinate to a superordinate domain name object. For example, ns1.example.com is subordinate to example.com. EPP actions that would not preserve this relationship MUST be explicitly disallowed.

A host can also be external: it can be created in a repository where no superordinate domain exists, such as ns1.example.com created in the .example repository so that DNS domains there can be delegated to it. Whether a host is internal or external depends on the repository in which it is used for delegation.

A host such as ns1.example1.com can serve as a name server for example2.com. In that case it MUST still be treated as an internal host, subject to the rules for subordinate hosts in the same repository.
sections.eli5: A computer's name often hangs under a bigger family name, like a child under a parent. If the child's name belongs to another family's registry, it is called an outsider there.

sections.title: Host Attributes and Status Values
sections.content:
Host names MUST conform to RFC 952 as updated by RFC 1123. IP addresses MUST follow the IPv4 and IPv6 syntax from RFC 791 and RFC 4291. A server MAY reject addresses that IANA has not allocated for public use. Dates and times MUST be in UTC, in the extended form with upper case T and Z.

A host object MUST always have at least one status value. Only the sponsoring client and the server may set them. Values starting with client can be changed by the client, values starting with server by the server, and others are server-managed. A client MUST NOT alter status values set by the server.

Some combinations are forbidden: ok may be combined only with linked, linked may be combined with any status, the four pending values MUST NOT be combined with each other, and pendingDelete and pendingUpdate cannot be combined with the matching delete or update prohibitions.
sections.eli5: Each entry wears one or more sticker labels, like Locked or Waiting. Some stickers only the owner can stick on, and some only the registry can, and a few stickers cannot be worn together.

sections.title: The Commands
sections.content:
Two query commands work on hosts. <check> asks whether one or more host names can be provisioned and returns an avail value of 1/true or 0/false, with an optional reason. <info> returns the name, a repository object identifier, status values, any IP addresses, the sponsoring and creating clients, and dates.

<create> takes a name and zero or more addresses, each marked v4 (the default) or v6. IP addresses are REQUIRED only as needed to produce DNS glue records. If the host name is in a namespace the server is authoritative for, the superordinate domain MUST already be known to the server.

<update> can add or remove addresses and statuses and can change the host name. Changing an external host that has associations with objects sponsored by a different client MUST fail with error 2305.

<delete> SHOULD NOT be used while the host is still associated with another object, since that can break DNS resolution for domains that refer to it.
sections.eli5: You can ask if a name is free, look up its details, add a new one, change it or remove it. Before you throw one away, make sure nobody is still using it.

sections.title: Transfers, Renewals and Offline Review
sections.content:
There is no direct <renew> or <transfer> for hosts. Hosts are transferred implicitly when their superordinate domain is transferred, and a host's trDate is recorded only then.

A server operator MAY review a transform command offline. The server then answers with result code 1001, meaning the command was processed but the action is pending, and the object's status MUST include the matching pending value, for example pendingCreate. When review ends, the server MUST notify the client with a service message, which carries a panData element whose paResult attribute says whether the request was approved or denied.

A transform attempted by an unauthorized client MUST be rejected with code 2201.
sections.eli5: Sometimes a person at the registry wants to look at your request first. They tell you right away that it is waiting, and later they leave you a note saying yes or no.

sections.title: Internationalization and Security
sections.content:
EPP is XML, so it supports Unicode, and UTF-8 is RECOMMENDED where parsers disagree on encodings. Host names must follow RFC 952 and RFC 1123, and the text notes that RFC 3490 describes using ASCII labels to represent non-ASCII ones, with a warning that these requirements might change.

The security section is short. The host mapping provides no security services and adds no considerations beyond those in RFC 5730 or those of the protocol layers EPP runs on.
sections.eli5: Names can be written in many alphabets, and the rules say how to do it safely. Locking the doors is handled by the main EPP rulebook, not this chapter.

sections.title: Changes from RFC 4932
sections.content: The appendix lists eight small changes. References were updated, such as RFC 5730 replacing RFC 4930, and RFC 3596 replacing RFC 1886. Two text additions were made: other notification methods MAY be used in addition to the required service message, and text about response code 2201 was added. BSD license text was also added to the XML schema section.
sections.eli5: The new version is mostly the old one with fixed references and a couple of extra sentences.

items.label: Normal
items.desc: No pending operations or prohibitions; may be combined only with linked.

items.label: In use
items.desc: At least one active association with another object, such as a domain.

items.label: No delete
items.desc: Requests to delete the object MUST be rejected.

items.label: No update
items.desc: Updates other than removing this status MUST be rejected.

items.label: Action pending
items.desc: A command was processed but the server has not completed the action.
